prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

You asked me once, on our way back from the midmorning trip to the spring: “What do you hate, and who do you love?” And I answered, from behind the eyelashes of my surprise, my blood rushing like the shadow cast by a cloud of starlings: “I hate departure . . . I love the spring and the path to the spring, and I worship the middle hours of morning.” And you laughed . . . and the almond tree blossomed and the thicket grew loud with nightingales. . . . A question now four decades old: I salute that question’s answer; and an answer as old as your departure; I salute that answer’s question . . . And today, it’s preposterous, here we are at a friendly airport by the slimmest of chances, and we meet. Ah, Lord! we meet. And here you are asking—again, it’s absolutely preposterous— I recognized you but you didn’t recognize me. “Is it you?!” But you wouldn’t believe it. And suddenly you burst out and asked: “If you’re really you, What do you hate and who do you love?!” And I answered— my blood fleeing the hall, rushing in me like the shadow cast by a cloud of starlings: “I hate departure, and I love the spring, and the path to the spring, and I worship the middle hours of morning.” And you wept, and flowers bowed their heads, and doves in the silk of their sorrow stumbled.

outputs.L1:
You once asked me, on our way back from the midmorning journey to the spring, “What do you hate, and whom do you love?” And I answered, from behind the lashes of my surprise, my blood rushing like the shadow cast by a cloud of starlings: “I hate departure . . . I love the spring and the path to the spring, and I worship the middle hours of morning.”

And you laughed . . . and the almond tree blossomed, and the thicket grew loud with nightingales. . . .

A question now four decades old: I salute that question’s answer. And an answer as old as your departure: I salute that answer’s question. . . .

And today—preposterously—here we are, at a friendly airport, brought together by the slimmest of chances, and we meet. Ah, Lord! We meet.

And here you are, asking again—it is utterly preposterous. I recognized you, but you did not recognize me.

“Is it you?!”

But you would not believe it. Then, suddenly, you burst out and asked, “If you are truly you, what do you hate, and whom do you love?!”

And I answered—my blood fleeing the hall, rushing through me like the shadow cast by a cloud of starlings: “I hate departure, and I love the spring and the path to the spring, and I worship the middle hours of morning.”

And you wept, and the flowers bowed their heads, and the doves stumbled in the silk of their sorrow.
outputs.L2:
Once, as we returned from our late-morning visit to the spring, you asked me, “What do you despise, and whom do you love?” Startled, I looked out from beneath my lashes, while my blood surged like the moving darkness beneath a flock of starlings. I replied, “I despise leaving. I love the spring and the road that leads to it, and I adore the hours at the heart of the morning.” You laughed then; the almond tree opened into bloom, and the nightingales filled the thicket with song.

That question was asked forty years ago. I honor the answer it received—and that answer, now as old as the day you left, honors the question that called it forth.

And now, by the most unlikely accident, we find each other again in a welcoming airport. Dear God, after all this time, we meet. Absurdly, unbelievably, you ask once more. I knew you immediately, though you failed to know me.

“Can it really be you?” you said, unable to accept it. Then, all at once, you cried out: “If you truly are who you claim to be, tell me: what do you despise, and whom do you love?”

As the blood seemed to drain from the terminal and race through my body like the shadow of starlings crossing the earth, I answered, “I despise leaving. I love the spring and the road that leads to it, and I adore the middle hours of the morning.”

Then you began to weep. The flowers lowered their faces, and the doves faltered within the silken folds of their grief.
outputs.L3:
Four decades earlier, the speaker had been asked a simple but revealing question: what did they hate, and what did they love? Their answer was memorable. They hated departure, loved the spring and every path that led toward it, and worshipped the quiet middle hours of the morning.

After many years of separation, the two met again by chance at an airport. Time had changed them so much that the other person did not recognize the speaker at first. Searching for certainty, they repeated the same question they had asked forty years before. The speaker responded with the very same words: they hated departure, loved the spring and the road to it, and worshipped the middle hours of morning.

At once, recognition broke through the distance of the years. The familiar answer awakened memories long buried, and the reunion became charged with grief, tenderness, and remembrance.
outputs.L4:
Forty years after their separation, the speaker unexpectedly meets his former beloved at an airport. The chance reunion collapses the distance between past and present: amid the bustle of travelers and the inevitability of another departure, he remembers a question she asked him long ago. Her words had joined love with the imagery of spring, morning, and the road ahead—images of renewal and hope that were nevertheless shadowed by parting.

Now, after decades apart, she asks him the same question again. His answer has not changed. He still hates departure, yet he still loves the spring, the freshness of morning, and the path along which life continues. The repetition reveals that time has altered neither his deepest feelings nor the memory of what they once shared. Though their lives have followed separate courses, his love has endured quietly beneath the passing years. Hearing this unchanged answer, the beloved is moved to tears, recognizing that their bond has survived distance, age, and loss.

**You, What, and And**

You are the beginning of a question.

What is the word that opens the door to curiosity.

And is the bridge that connects one thought, one person, and one possibility to another.

Together, these words form a simple invitation: **You—what will you discover, and where will it lead?**

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poetic monologue about unexpectedly meeting a lost love at an airport forty years after they first asked, “What do you hate, and who do you love?” Repeat the original answer as the proof of identity.
counterfactuals.output:
The airport was all glass and weather,  
all silver announcements drifting down  
like snow that could not touch the ground.

I was standing beneath DEPARTURES,  
though I had nowhere left to leave,  
when I saw you—

forty years older,  
carrying your face carefully  
through the crowd.

You looked at me as one looks  
through a rain-streaked window:  
hoping, doubting,  
afraid the heart has mistaken  
a stranger for a country.

Then you asked it again.

Not hello.  
Not where have you been.  
Not why didn’t you write,  
or marry me,  
or come back before our hair  
became the color of distance.

You asked,

“What do you hate, and who do you love?”

And suddenly we were twenty,  
sitting on the hood of your father’s car,  
the summer dark around us,  
your question held between two heartbeats.

I had answered carelessly then,  
not knowing a sentence could outlive  
addresses, marriages, wars,  
the deaths of dogs and parents,  
the slow closing of familiar shops.

So I gave it to you again,  
word for word,  
the old password to the vanished world:

“I hate clocks, because they steal without hands,  
and I love you, because you give everything back.”

Your suitcase fell over.

Around us, flights were boarding,  
names were being called,  
whole lives were lifting into cloud.

But you smiled—

and forty years,  
that tireless thief,  
returned us to ourselves.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a surreal, nostalgic prose poem in which two former lovers reunite by chance after four decades. Include a childhood path to a spring, the middle hours of morning, a cloud of starlings, and mourning doves.
counterfactuals.output:
They met by accident in the middle hours of morning, when the day had opened its eyes but had not yet remembered its name.

Forty years stood between them like a house abandoned to weather. Still, she knew him by the way he paused beneath the clock tower, listening—as if time were water running underground. He knew her by the blue scarf at her throat, though the blue had once belonged to a summer dress, and the scarf had not yet been woven.

They said each other’s names. The names rose between them, startled birds.

Beyond the town, the childhood path to the spring was waiting under nettles and foxglove. They walked there without deciding, past the ruined mill, past the field where a cloud of starlings lifted and turned, lifted and turned, one dark thought changing its mind in the sky.

The path remembered their feet. It remembered them at twelve, at seventeen, barefoot and immortal, carrying tin cups and secrets. At the spring, the water still spoke in its small silver language. He knelt to drink and saw, reflected beside his weathered face, the boy he had been. She touched the surface, and rings moved outward through all the vanished years: marriages, funerals, cities, letters never sent.

“Were we happy?” he asked.

“We were young,” she said, which was not an answer, though it held one.

In the trees, mourning doves repeated their soft, broken arithmetic. Four decades, four decades, they seemed to say, and then: home, home.

For a moment the woods filled with impossible things—their bicycles leaning against an elm, her mother calling from a window long demolished, his old dog shaking rain from its coat. The spring ran upward toward its source. The starlings became stars.

They stood close, not touching, while their younger selves slipped past them down the path, laughing, late for a future that had already happened.

Then the clock in town struck eleven.

She smiled. He lifted his hand. And the morning, unable to keep them, folded their shadows together and carried them separately away.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an emotionally charged reunion scene in the style of a translated Arabic prose poem: the narrator recognizes an old beloved at an airport, but must answer a question from their shared past before being recognized in return.
counterfactuals.output:
At the airport, where every face was departing from another face, I saw her.

She stood beneath the blue light of the arrivals board, holding a small suitcase like someone holding the hand of a child who has forgotten the way home. Time had passed over her gently and without mercy. There was silver at her temples. There were countries in her eyes.

I said her name.

She turned, but did not know me.

How could she? The years had changed my face as exile changes the names of streets. My beard carried winters she had not witnessed. My shoulders had learned the language of closed doors.

She looked at me with the courtesy we offer strangers.

“Do I know you?”

The question entered my chest and found the old wound still awake.

I wanted to say: You knew me before sorrow became my profession. You knew me when my hands were empty except for your letters. You knew the boy who waited beneath your balcony and counted the lamps going dark across the city.

But she raised one finger, as she used to when memory demanded silence.

“Once,” she said slowly, “I asked someone a question. He never answered.”

Around us, wheels scraped the floor. Children ran into the arms of fathers. Loudspeakers called the names of distant cities, each one sounding like a door being locked.

“What question?” I whispered, though I knew.

Her eyes narrowed, searching the ruins of my face.

“If we met again after many years,” she said, “and I had forgotten you—how would you prove who you were?”

I closed my eyes.

There it was: the summer roof, the sleeping houses, the moon caught in the water tank. Her hair smelled of jasmine and dust. She had asked me laughing, yet fear trembled beneath her laughter, because even then we knew happiness was a guest who never unpacked.

I had kissed her palm instead of answering.

Now I opened my eyes.

“I would not tell you my name,” I said. “I would tell you where you hid your tears.”

Her breath stopped.

I stepped closer, but not close enough to frighten the years between us.

“Behind the blue door of your father’s house,” I continued, “there was a crack in the wall shaped like a river. You used to press your forehead against it when you cried, so no one would hear. You told me the wall carried your sorrow underground, beneath the city, all the way to the sea.”

Her suitcase fell.

For a moment she stood utterly still, as if recognition were not a light but a blade passing through her.

Then she said the name I had not heard in her voice for half a lifetime.

My name—broken, astonished, alive.

I answered, “Yes.”

And she struck my chest with both hands.

Once.

Twice.

For every letter unanswered. For every border. For the wedding that did not happen. For the dead who had left us to explain ourselves.

Then her fists opened, and she clung to my coat.

I held her.

The airport vanished.

No glass. No guards. No countries dividing the earth into permitted griefs. Only her face against my heart, listening for the young man buried there.

“You took too long,” she said.

“I was lost.”

“You knew the way.”

“Yes.”

“Then why?”

I had crossed oceans and rehearsed a thousand answers, but love, when it returns, makes liars of all explanations.

So I told her the only truth that remained.

“I was afraid you would remember me.”

She lifted her face. Tears had returned her eyes to the eyes I knew.

“And I,” she said, “was afraid I would not.”

Above us, another flight arrived.

Around us, strangers embraced as if the world had been forgiven.

She touched my cheek with the same hand I had kissed beneath the old moon, and the years, those stern customs officers, searched us one last time.

Finding nothing left to confiscate, they let us pass.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
